title: The rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19–31)
hook: a beggar at the gate has a name; the rich man doesn't

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shrewd manager, and a warning that you cannot serve God and mammon. Your line was faithful in little. Who did you spend a little on? Day five hundred sixty-one.

Think about the people you pass every day without knowing their names. The man who sells the newspaper. The woman who cleans the office after everyone goes home. Someone sitting by the same doorway each morning with a paper cup. You'd recognize their faces anywhere. Ask you their names and you'd have nothing. Jesus tells a story about a gate, and two men on either side of it. One of them gets a name. It's the only time in all his parables that a character is named, and it isn't the one you'd expect.

In the King James Bible: "There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day." Purple dye was so costly it was the color of kings. This man dressed like royalty and feasted daily. "And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, which was laid at his gate, full of sores." Laid there, as if someone carried him because he couldn't walk. He longs for the crumbs from the table, and the only ones who come near him are the street dogs, licking his sores. Lazarus is a form of the Hebrew name Eleazar, which means God has helped. Nobody else is helping him. The rich man, meanwhile, has no name at all. Later tradition called him Dives, but that's just the Latin word for rich. Both men die. Lazarus is carried by angels to Abraham's side; the rich man is in torment. And here's the detail that stings. The rich man calls across to Abraham: send Lazarus to cool my tongue. He knew his name. All those years, stepping past the gate, he knew exactly who was lying there. The story never says he kicked him or cursed him. He just didn't see him as someone who was his to help. Abraham answers that a great gulf is now fixed between them. The rich man begs for Lazarus to warn his five brothers. Abraham says they have Moses and the prophets. And the last line: "neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead." Christians differ on how literally to read the afterlife scenes here; many take it as a parable, not a map. But all agree on the gate. The gulf began there.
screen: then, large: `A CERTAIN BEGGAR NAMED LAZARUS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn a name. Settle and breathe. Picture your ordinary route through a day: the street, the shop, the bus, the building where you work. Who do you pass, again and again, without knowing their name? The cleaner, the security guard, the man at the corner, the cashier with the tired smile. Let their faces come up one by one. Choose one. Today, or the next time you see them, ask their name, and tell them yours. If you pray, you can pray for them by name afterward. The bell holds the time.
The rich man and Lazarus. A rich man with no name, a beggar at his gate named God has helped, and a gulf that began long before either of them died.

howItsDone: This parable has shaped Christian care for the poor for centuries; many churches run street outreach that begins with learning people's names, and Christians often read it when thinking about wealth and those at their own gate.

myth: the Bible names the rich man Dives
Luke gives him no name. Dives is just the Latin word for rich, used by later tradition.
Lazarus is the only named character in Jesus' parables
every other parable character is a certain man, a woman, a shepherd. this one has a name.
the rich man didn't know who Lazarus was
in the story he asks for Lazarus by name. he knew him all along.

fork.setup: the rich man, in torment, begs Abraham to send Lazarus to warn his five brothers. what does Abraham say?
options: yes, Lazarus will go at once.
they have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them.
fork.reveal: "they have Moses and the prophets." and if they won't hear them, "neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead."

original.note: Hebrew: Eleazar, God has helped. Lazarus is its Greek form.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about heaven and hell.
what it means: a story about a gate: a man who knew the beggar's name and never saw him as his to help.
what a scholar hears: Lazarus, from Eleazar, God has helped, is the only named character in Jesus' parables, and the rich man's name, Dives, is only Latin for rich.

notes: Lazarus as the only named character in Jesus' parables: widely stated. Confirm.
Lazarus from Hebrew Eleazar ('God has helped'): standard. Confirm Hebrew spelling and pronunciation.
'Laid at his gate' (ἐβέβλητο, 'had been thrown/laid'): the inference that he was carried is common; confirm.
Afterlife: 'Christians differ on how literally to read the afterlife scenes' is stated without ranking. Abraham's bosom paraphrased as 'Abraham's side'.
